questions.question: A constantan wire has cross-sectional area 3.97 x 10^-7 m^2. Its breaking stress is about 420 MPa. Deduce whether the wire can support a weight of 150 N.
questions.answer: Yes. Stress = 3.78 x 10^8 Pa (378 MPa), which is less than the breaking stress of 420 MPa.
steps: Stress = force / cross-sectional area.
Compare this with the breaking stress of 420 MPa.
378 MPa is less than 420 MPa, so the wire does not break and can support 150 N.

questions.question: Using the force against extension graph for the constantan wire, show that the stiffness of the wire is about 1.3 x 10^4 N/m.
questions.answer: Stiffness = gradient of the straight part of the graph = 60 N / 4.6 x 10^-3 m = 1.3 x 10^4 N m^-1
steps: Stiffness k = F / x, which is the gradient of the force-extension graph in its straight-line (elastic) region.
Take a large triangle on the straight part, from the origin to the point (4.6 mm, 60 N); convert the extension to metres: 4.6 x 10^-3 m.
This is about 1.3 x 10^4 N m^-1, as required.

questions.question: The stiffness k is related to the Young modulus E by k = EA/x, where x is the unstretched length and A is the cross-sectional area. Using k = 1.3 x 10^4 N/m, x = 4.00 m and A = 3.97 x 10^-7 m^2, determine the Young modulus of constantan.
steps: Rearrange the stiffness relation k = EA/x to give E = kx / A.
Young modulus of constantan = 1.3 x 10^11 Pa.

questions.question: A climber of weight 650 N is suspended on a rope in a Tyrolean traverse. Using the free-body force diagram, show that the tension in the rope is about 1.3 x 10^3 N.
steps: The climber is in equilibrium, so the upward components of the two rope tensions balance the weight of 650 N.
Each rope makes 76 deg with the vertical, so each has a vertical component T cos76.

questions.question: The rope has an unstretched length of 120 m. Determine the strain in the rope while it supports the climber, ignoring the weight of the rope.
questions.answer: Strain = 0.031 (3.1 x 10^-2): the stretched length is 123.7 m, an extension of 3.7 m over 120 m
steps: Each half of the rope spans 60 m horizontally (half of the 120 m gap) and makes 76 deg with the vertical.
Length of one half = 60 / sin76 = 61.8 m, so the stretched length of the rope = 2 x 61.8 = 123.7 m.
Extension = 123.7 - 120 = 3.7 m.
Strain = extension / original length = 3.7 / 120 = 0.031.

questions.question: The rope has cross-sectional area 3.14 x 10^-4 m^2. Using the tension and the strain from earlier parts, determine the Young modulus of the rope material.
steps: Tension in the rope T = 1.34 x 10^3 N (from part (a)).
Strain = 0.031 (from part (b)(i)).
Young modulus = stress / strain = 4.3 x 10^6 / 0.031 = 1.4 x 10^8 Pa.

questions.question: Which of the following gives the Young modulus of a material from its tensile stress-strain graph? Options: A area under the line up to the breaking point; B area under the line up to the elastic limit; C gradient of the tangent to the line at the origin; D stress divided by strain at the breaking point.
questions.answer: C: the gradient of the tangent to the line at the origin (the straight-line, elastic region).
steps: Young modulus E = stress / strain in the linear, elastic region.
On a stress-strain graph this ratio is the gradient of the straight-line part at the origin.
Areas under the graph give the work done per unit volume, so A and B are wrong.
D uses the breaking point, which is not in the linear region, so C is correct.

questions.question: A student determines the Young modulus of copper by adding known masses and measuring extensions. Which other quantities should be measured directly? Options: A diameter and mass of the wire; B diameter and original length of the wire; C radius and mass of the wire; D radius and original length of the wire.
questions.answer: B: diameter and original length of the wire.
steps: Young modulus E = (F / A) / (x / L), so the area, original length, force and extension are needed.
The force comes from the known masses, and the extension is measured directly, so the mass of the wire is not needed.
The area needs the diameter, which is measured directly with a micrometer; radius is not measured directly.
The original length L is needed for the strain, so the answer is B.

questions.question: A student determines the Young modulus of copper using a copper wire. Describe how the diameter of the wire should be determined.
questions.answer: Use a micrometer screw gauge at several positions along the wire and in several orientations, then use the mean diameter.
steps: Use a micrometer screw gauge, which reads the diameter to about 0.01 mm.
Measure the diameter at several positions along the wire to check it is uniform.
At each position, take readings in several orientations to check the cross-section is circular.
Calculate the mean diameter from all readings, after correcting for any zero error, for use in the area calculation.

questions.question: Using the load-extension graph, the original length of 2.4 m and the diameter of 2.3 x 10^-4 m, determine the Young modulus of copper.
steps: From the straight part of the graph, take a large triangle, e.g. the point (2.0 x 10^-3 m, 4.5 N): gradient = F / x = 4.5 / 2.0 x 10^-3 = 2.25 x 10^3 N m^-1.
Cross-sectional area A = pi d^2 / 4 = pi x (2.3 x 10^-4)^2 / 4 = 4.15 x 10^-8 m^2.
Young modulus E = (F / A) / (x / L) = gradient x L / A.

questions.question: Explain why the sample of wire used in the copper experiment should be long and thin.
questions.answer: Long and thin wires give a larger extension for a given load, so the extension is measured with a smaller percentage uncertainty and the wire stays in its elastic region.
steps: The extension must be measured accurately, and the reading uncertainty is roughly fixed in size.
Extension = strain x L, so a longer wire gives a larger extension for the same strain.
Stress = F / A, so a thin wire (small A) has a larger stress for the same load.
A larger stress gives a larger strain and hence a larger extension, which reduces the percentage uncertainty in x.
The load can then be kept small enough that the stress stays within the elastic limit.
Within the elastic limit, the stress-strain relation is linear, so a valid value of the Young modulus can be found from the gradient.

questions.question: State the meaning of the term Young modulus.
questions.answer: Young modulus is the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain within the limit of proportionality (elastic region), measured in Pa.
steps: Stress = force / cross-sectional area, and strain = extension / original length.
Young modulus E = stress / strain, for a material within its elastic region.
It is a property of the material and is measured in pascals (N m^-2).
It equals the gradient of the straight-line part of the stress-strain graph.

questions.question: The student repeated the diameter measurements at different positions and orientations. Using the results table, determine the cross-sectional area of the wire.
questions.answer: A = 4.3 x 10^-8 m^2 (mean diameter 0.234 mm)
steps: Take the mean of the four diameters: (0.230 + 0.235 + 0.230 + 0.240) / 4 = 0.234 mm = 2.34 x 10^-4 m.
Area of a circle: A = pi d^2 / 4.

questions.question: The graph of mass m against extension x has gradient 195 kg/m for a copper sample of length 3.50 m. Determine the Young modulus of the copper.
steps: For the wire, F = mg = (EA / L) x, so m = (EA / (gL)) x and the gradient of m against x is EA / (gL).
Rearranging, E = gradient x g x L / A.
E = 195 x 9.81 x 3.50 / 4.29 x 10^-8 (using A from part (b)(i)).

questions.topic: Effect Of Wire Length On Gradient
questions.question: Another student repeats the experiment using a 2.00 m length of the same copper wire. Suggest how the gradient and the Young modulus obtained will differ from the first student's values.
questions.answer: The gradient will be larger (about 1.75 times, since it is inversely proportional to length), but the Young modulus will be the same.
steps: For the wire, F = mg = (EA / L) x, so m = (EA / (gL)) x.
The gradient of m against x is EA / (gL), which is inversely proportional to the length L.
The 2.00 m wire is shorter than 3.50 m, so its gradient is larger, by a factor 3.50 / 2.00 = 1.75.
The Young modulus is a property of the material, so it is unchanged, provided the same copper wire is used.

questions.question: State a suitable measuring instrument to measure the diameter of a titanium alloy sample of diameter 5.05 mm.
questions.answer: A micrometer screw gauge.
steps: The diameter is 5.05 mm and must be measured to about 0.01 mm.
A micrometer screw gauge has a resolution of 0.01 mm, which is suitable.
A metre rule has a resolution of only 1 mm, which is too coarse.
So a micrometer screw gauge is the suitable instrument.

questions.question: Using the stress-strain graph for the titanium alloy sample (original length 40.0 cm), determine the Young modulus of the sample.
questions.answer: E = gradient of the linear part = 1.2 x 10^11 Pa (about 120 GPa)
steps: Young modulus = stress / strain = the gradient of the straight (linear) part of the graph.
Take a large triangle on the straight section, e.g. stress 600 MPa at strain 0.0050.
E = 600 x 10^6 Pa / 0.0050 = 1.2 x 10^11 Pa (the original length is not needed, since strain is already given).

questions.question: The titanium alloy sample breaks at point B on the stress-strain graph. Determine the force required to break the sample, using its 5.05 mm diameter.
steps: At point B the stress on the graph is about 1290 MPa = 1.29 x 10^9 Pa.
Cross-sectional area A = pi d^2 / 4 = pi x (5.05 x 10^-3)^2 / 4 = 2.0 x 10^-5 m^2.
Force = stress x area = 1.29 x 10^9 x 2.0 x 10^-5 = 2.6 x 10^4 N (accept a small range, since the stress is read from the graph).

questions.question: Show that the area under the linear part of a stress-strain graph represents the work done per unit volume in stretching the sample.
questions.answer: Work per unit volume = (1/2) x stress x strain, which is the area of the triangle under the linear graph.
steps: In the linear region the force rises uniformly from 0 to F, so the average force is F/2 and W = (1/2) F x.
The volume of the sample is V = A L.
Work per unit volume W / V = (1/2)(F/A)(x/L) = (1/2) x stress x strain.
The area under the linear stress-strain graph is a triangle of base strain and height stress, which is (1/2) x stress x strain, so the area is the work per unit volume.

questions.question: Using the fact that the area under a stress-strain graph gives work done per unit volume, estimate the work required to break the titanium alloy sample.
questions.answer: About 5 x 10^2 J (500 J)
steps: The area under the curve up to B is the work done per unit volume. Estimate it by splitting the area into strips (trapezoids) or counting squares.
Area from strain 0 to 0.0563 (to B): about 0.0563 x an average stress of roughly 1100 MPa, which is about 6.3 x 10^7 J m^-3 (6.3 x 10^7 Pa).
Volume of the sample = A L = 2.0 x 10^-5 m^2 x 0.400 m = 8.0 x 10^-6 m^3.
Work = work per unit volume x volume = 6.3 x 10^7 x 8.0 x 10^-6 = 5 x 10^2 J (accept about 450 to 550 J).

questions.question: A copper wire is clamped at one end, passed over a pulley and loaded with masses at the other end, with a metre rule and marker. Describe the other measurements needed and how they determine the Young modulus, defining any symbols used.
questions.answer: Measure the original length L and the extension x for each load; plot F = mg against x, giving gradient EA/L, so E = gradient x L / A, where A = pi d^2 / 4.
steps: Measure the original length L of the wire from the clamp to the marker, using the metre rule.
For each added mass m, the force F = mg, where g is the gravitational field strength (9.81 m/s^2).
Read the marker position on the metre rule before and after loading; the extension x is the change in position.
Plot F against x; the gradient k = F / x = EA / L, where k is the stiffness and A the cross-sectional area.
Calculate A = pi d^2 / 4 from the measured diameter d.
Young modulus E = (gradient x L) / A, since E = stress / strain = (F / A) / (x / L).

questions.question: A 5.0 N weight is attached to a copper wire of diameter 0.56 mm and length 2.5 m. The Young modulus of copper is 1.1 x 10^11 Pa. Calculate the extension of the wire.
questions.answer: Extension = 4.6 x 10^-4 m (0.46 mm).
steps: Cross-sectional area A = pi (d/2)^2 = pi x (2.8 x 10^-4 m)^2 = 2.46 x 10^-7 m^2.
Extension = strain x length = 1.85 x 10^-4 x 2.5 m = 4.6 x 10^-4 m (0.46 mm).

questions.question: Using a micrometer to measure the diameter of a wire, describe how the student should check that the wire is uniform and has a circular cross-section.
questions.answer: Measure the diameter at several positions along the wire (uniform), and at each position measure in several orientations (circular).
steps: To check uniformity, measure the diameter at several positions along the length of the wire.
If the readings agree, the diameter is uniform along the wire.
To check the cross-section is circular, at one position measure the diameter in several orientations, turning the wire between readings.
If the diameter is the same in every orientation, the cross-section is circular.

questions.question: The student kept his feet away from the apparatus so that masses could not fall on them. Explain one other safety precaution for this practical.
questions.answer: Wear safety goggles, since the wire may snap and flying pieces or the masses could strike the eyes.
steps: The wire may snap under load, releasing stored energy and sending the masses or wire backwards.
Eye protection such as safety goggles protects the eyes from flying pieces.
Do not load the wire beyond its breaking load or elastic limit, which reduces the chance of snapping.
Keep clear of the masses and hanger area when adding masses, and place a guard under the masses if available.

questions.question: Each time more mass is added, the extension increases by a few mm. Explain why a vernier scale should be used to measure x instead of a metre rule.
questions.answer: A vernier scale resolves about 0.1 mm, while a metre rule resolves about 1 mm, so the percentage uncertainty in a few mm extension is much smaller with the vernier.
steps: The extension x is only a few mm, which is small compared with the metre rule's scale divisions.
A metre rule has a resolution of about 1 mm, so its reading uncertainty is a large fraction of x.
A vernier scale has a resolution of about 0.1 mm, so its percentage uncertainty is much smaller.
A smaller uncertainty in x gives a more accurate gradient and hence a more accurate Young modulus.

questions.question: Using the force-extension graph, the wire length of 1.80 m and the diameter of 0.17 mm, deduce which material in the table the wire is made from.
questions.answer: Brass: E = 1.07 x 10^11 Pa (about 106 GPa)
steps: The graph is straight but does not pass through the origin (zero extension at 1 N), so use the gradient, not a single point: gradient = delta-x / F = (10.4 - 0) x 10^-3 / (15 - 1) = 7.4 x 10^-4 m N^-1.
E = 1.07 x 10^11 Pa = 107 GPa, which matches brass (106 GPa), not aluminium (68 GPa) or steel (200 GPa).

questions.question: Two wires of the same material are tested. The second wire has a larger extension before breaking. Which of the following produced this result? Options: A the second wire had a greater diameter; B the second wire had a longer length; C the second wire had a smaller diameter; D the second wire had a shorter length.
questions.answer: B: the second wire had a longer length.
steps: Both wires are the same material, so they break at the same breaking strain.
Extension at breaking = breaking strain x original length.
A longer wire therefore has a larger extension before breaking.
Diameter does not change the breaking strain, so A and C are wrong, and D would reduce the extension, so B is correct.
